headline: Scientists Discover T. Rex Had Human-Like Body Temperature
meta_description: A 66-million-year-old fossilized tooth reveals T. rex maintained a body temperature of 97°F, nearly identical to humans, proving the giant predator was warm-bl…
summary_short: Chemical analysis of a T. rex tooth from 66 million years ago shows the dinosaur ran at 97°F—about human body temperature—offering the first direct evidence of its warm-…
body:
Scientists have done something that once seemed impossible: they have effectively taken the temperature of a Tyrannosaurus rex that died 66 million years ago. Using fossilized teeth from Thomas, the most complete tyrannosaur skeleton at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, UCLA researchers discovered that T. rex maintained a body temperature of about 97 degrees Fahrenheit—nearly identical to modern humans. The finding, published in September 2026 in Science Advances, provides the first actual temperature measurement for the ancient predator, offering direct evidence that it was warm-blooded rather than cold-blooded like many modern reptiles.

The breakthrough relied on a refined technique that took UCLA scientists over a decade to perfect. The method analyzes microscopic chemical bonds of rare carbon and oxygen isotopes preserved in tooth enamel. These bonds form differently depending on temperature: warmer animals leave fewer of these bonds than colder ones. What made the discovery possible was a dramatic improvement in the technique that reduced the amount of tooth material needed for testing by roughly 90 percent—finally allowing scientists to study irreplaceable museum specimens without causing significant damage.

The implications extend beyond a single number. A warm-blooded T. rex explains how the predator stayed active while hunting or scavenging for food, and it also clarifies how tyrannosaurs survived in inhospitable colder regions, including as far north as Alaska. The 97-degree reading positions T. rex between modern cold-blooded reptiles, which maintain temperatures around 82-86 degrees Fahrenheit, and birds—the evolutionary descendants of dinosaurs—which often reach 104-109 degrees. It reveals T. rex as an energetic, metabolically active animal built for an active life: a creature far removed from the sluggish, sun-dependent reptile of earlier scientific imagination.
quick_facts: T. rex body temperature: 97°F, nearly identical to humans
UCLA perfected technique reduced tooth sample needed by 90%
Specimen studied: Thomas, most complete tyrannosaur skeleton in LA
Research published September 2026 in Science Advances journal
T. rex fossils found as far north as Alaska
